🍎 Lesson plan · 🤿 Deep dive · Lesson 7

Lesson plan: How Computers See

How a picture turns into numbers, and how a network finds edges, shapes and objects in them.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • explain how a picture becomes a grid of numbers (pixels, greyscale and RGB);
  • describe how a filter slides over a picture to find edges (a convolution);
  • explain how a CNN builds up from edges to objects, and why vision models can be fooled.

Warm-up

Zoom into a photo as far as you can. What do you see in the end?

If you can, zoom into a photo on the projector until the squares appear. Then ask: how could a computer store each square?

Reading

Students read the lesson “How Computers See”. Students look for what 0 and 255 mean, what a filter does, and what an adversarial example is.

Activity: Mini-lab “Pixel detective”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 7 and pick the shape “Square”.
  2. They try the three filters (vertical edges, horizontal edges, blur) and read the sentence under the result each time.
  3. They point at one square of the result and check its sum by hand: multiply square by square, then add up.
  4. They fill in the worksheet's table for the other shapes, then paint a picture of their own.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers paint a picture that the vertical-edge filter finds but the horizontal-edge filter misses completely, and explain why it works.

Discussion questions

  • Face unlock works well in daylight but worse in the dark. Why might that be?
  • Nobody writes a CNN's filters by hand. Where do they come from?
  • A few stickers on a stop sign can make a model misread it. What does that mean for cars that read road signs?
  • A vision model finds patterns, not meaning. What is the difference?

Exit ticket

In one sentence, explain what a filter does to a picture.

Quick check. Researchers added a faint pattern of noise to a photo of a panda. People still saw a panda, but the network said “gibbon”, and was very sure. What is a picture like this called?
Right answer: An adversarial example

Easier and harder

Easier. Before the mini-lab, draw a small grid of 0s and 1s and a 3 × 3 vertical-edge filter on the board, and work out two squares of the result together.

Harder. Students work out by hand what the blur filter gives at a corner of the square, as a fraction, and check it in the mini-lab.
